item.title: NPC - Master List
item.description:
📇 NPC Master List Role: Crime Lord / Smuggler Kingpin / Elite Hunter Associated PC: Ryan_Lockwood
Location: Subterranean Market, Chicago Underworld Rank: A-Rank Threat (Social/Resource), B-Rank Combatant (~350 Points) Key Details: Controls the smuggling of mana cores and illegal Gate artifacts in Chicago [1]. Motivation: Believes Ryan stole a specific Gate artifact handgun during a black-market auction, or is the person who did (Mistaken Identity) [1]. Tactics: Uses lieutenants and bribed DPS officials; wants Ryan alive for interrogation [1]. Loadout: Exotic magical firearms smuggled from Gates [2]. Role: Ancient Symbiote / Internal Antagonist
Associated PC: Lena_Kozlov Location: Inside Lena’s mind/soul (Possession) Rank: S-Rank Knowledge / Variable Power Key Details: Nature: Not an external enemy, but a "Possession Enemy." She is an ancient sorceress queen trying to "complete" Lena [3]. Trigger: Manifests when Lena is unconscious. [3]. Personality: Arrogant, regal. Views modern hunters as unworthy. Goal: To overwrite Lena eventually, but currently acts as a twisted mentor/guardian [4]. Role: Occult Terrorist Organization
Associated PC: Tessa_Thorpe Location: Global / Gate-Adjacent Rank: Faction Threat Key Details: Belief: They believe Tessa is the reincarnated vessel of their god, Koga Thun [5]. The Twist: They believe Tessa is corrupted by her modern humanity and lack of "necrotic" discipline. She must be killed/sacrificed to "free" the divine essence [6]. Assets: "Purifiers" (assassins), Familiar Spirits, Gate-born monstrosities [7]. Connection: Tessa carries a ring belonging to the cult [8]. Role: Final Guardian / Dungeon Anchor
Source: Dungeon of the Fire Opal Rank: High C / Borderline B
Gate Overlay: Gate Boss (C-Rank Limited) Key Stats & Traits: Origin: Undead Human (Opal-bound). A former guardian or noble who died protecting the Opal [9]. DR: 12–15 (Gate Aura). Abilities: Terror aura, Insubstantiality (Ghostly), Possession attempts [10]. Kill Condition: Must destroy or overload the Fire Opal anchor to defeat permanently [11]. Role: Elite Undead / Sub-Boss
Source: Dungeon of the Fire Opal (Original Module) Rank: C+ Traits: Applied Ghostly prefix to a Draugr stat block [10]. Possesses paralysis claws and a banshee-like scream [12]. Role: Opportunist / Interloper
Source: Dungeon of the Fire Opal (Room 12/Laboratory) Rank: C Key Details: Status: Living humanoid, not undead [13]. Motivation: Knows the Fire Opal exists and wants to steal/bargain for it. She is not loyal to the dungeon [14]. Tactics: Uses seals and wards to survive among the undead. Likely willing to trade intel with the PCs for safety or a cut of the loot [14]. Role: Merchants / Quest Givers
Location: Subterranean Market Notable Types: The Tattoo Artist: operates in "The Tattoo Tunnels." Provides emergency rune magic and painful one-shot buffs [15]. The Demolitions Guy: "Just packing up." Unofficial source for Lena’s explosives. Charges high prices [15]. Food Stall Vendors: Serve "Mana Broth" (restores 1 FP) and "Cold Barley Tea" (suppresses fear) [16]. Role: DPS / Suppression Point Total: ~150–200 Key Stats: ST: 11 | DX: 13 | IQ: 10 | HT: 11 Skill: Guns (Pistol/SMG)-14+, Fast-Draw-13. Gear: 9mm SMG or Heavy Pistol. Kevlar Vest (DR 8). Basic comms and dungeon survival kit. Tactics: Suppressive fire to strip Ablative DR from monsters so Mages can finish them [17]. Role: Recon / Traps Point Total: ~150–200 Key Stats: ST: 10 | DX: 14 | IQ: 11 | HT: 11 Skill: Stealth-14, Observation-13, Traps-12, Carbine-12. Gear: Suppressed Carbine or Crossbow. Light armor (mobility focus). Scanner/Sensor gear. Tactics: Identifies ambushes and high-threat targets (Mages/Leaders) for the team [17]. Role: Support / Utility Point Total: ~175 Key Traits: Magery 0 or 1 (Cannot use full syntactic trees). Abilities: Knows 1 Noun OR 1 Verb (e.g., "Create" or "Fire") for minor cantrips. Gear: Uses Wands or Scrolls to channel limited mana [18]. tags: database/npcs status/active type/master_list created: 2025-12-13

item.title: Threshold Overload
item.description: Threshold exceeded by a small amount.Effects represent magical fatigue and instability.Possible results:• caster loses FP equal to Threshold excess • temporary magical feedback (1–2 injury ignoring DR) • -1 to next spellcasting roll • visible magical aura / mana flareNarrative effect: The mage feels reality pushing back. Mana destabilizes the spell matrix.Possible effects:• uncontrolled spell surge • spell effect expands or shifts unpredictably • caster takes 1d injury ignoring DR • random nearby object affected by magicNarrative effect: Magic escapes the caster’s control. Reality violently rejects the spell.Possible effects:• spell explodes outward • caster stunned for 1d seconds • uncontrolled elemental manifestation • summon a minor Gate creature • magical shockwaveNarrative effect: The Gate energies tear through the battlefield. Extreme magical overload.Possible effects:• temporary Gate rift opens • summon powerful monster • catastrophic spell detonation • caster knocked unconscious • permanent magical mutation or corruptionNarrative effect: Reality cracks under magical pressure. You can tie severity to Threshold exceeded.Example:This system:• encourages powerful spells • creates risk for greedy casters • reinforces the Gate instability themeIt also matches the Solo Leveling vibe, where magic can spiral out of control.Tessa casts a huge spell.She exceeds Threshold by 5.Result:BreachPossible outcome: The fireball detonates early and a ring of flames spreads across the room. Instead of choosing effects, roll 1d6:Place this in:13_Magic_System └── Threshold └── Threshold Overload.md

item.title: Parameters
item.description: Parameters modify how a spell behaves after the Verb and College determine what the magic is doing.Parameters do not change the magical domain — they only adjust the delivery, shape, or persistence of the effect.Spell structure:Verb + College + ParametersExample:Create + Fire + MoveCreates a fire projectile.Allows the magical effect to travel or apply motion.Without Move, the spell occurs at the target point or target creature.Move allows effects to:• become projectiles • propel objects • push or pull targets • carry magic through spaceExamples:Create + Fire + MoveFirebolt projectileControl + Body + MoveTelekinetically lift or push a creatureControl + Earth + MoveAnimate or throw a stone or metal objectMoS spent on Move can determine:• projectile speed • guidance / tracking • force of telekinetic motionExpands the spell beyond a single target into multiple spaces.Area determines how many spaces are affected, while MoS determines the geometry.Area effects may take forms such as:• explosion • cone • beam / line • wall • zoneExamples:Create + Fire + AreaExplosionCreate + Air + AreaShockwaveCreate + Fire + Area + DurationFirewallExtends the distance at which the spell can be delivered.Without Range, spells use the default casting distance.Range allows spells to:• strike distant targets • project magic across large spaces • extend sensory spellsExample:Sense + Mind + RangeDetect thoughts at distanceCreate + Fire + RangeLong-range fireboltAllows the magical effect to persist over time.Without Duration, the spell resolves instantly.Duration is used for:• sustained buffs • lingering hazards • barriers • control effectsExamples:Protect + Body + DurationTemporary defensive enchantmentCreate + Fire + Area + DurationLingering firestormControl + Air + DurationSustained wind controlDefines the geometry of the magical construct.Shape is used when the spell must create structured forms rather than bursts.Examples include:• walls • barriers • blades • platforms • cagesExamples:Create + Earth + ShapeStone wallCreate + Force + ShapeMagical barrierCreate + Ice + ShapeIce spear or barrierTypical spells use:1 Verb 1 College 0–2 ParametersMore parameters increase casting complexity and casting time.Example progression:Create + Fire simple magical sparkCreate + Fire + Move fireboltCreate + Fire + Area fireball explosionCreate + Fire + Area + Duration firestorm

item.title: Margin of Success (MoS)
item.description: MoS represents the power budget of a spell.Players spend MoS to increase damage, area, duration, or control."A successful spell always produces a minimal effect even if MoS = 0.”Every successful spell generates a minimal baseline effect.MoS enhances this baseline.MoS represents the power budget of a spell.Players spend MoS to increase damage, area, duration, or control.Every successful spell generates a minimal baseline effect.MoS enhances this baseline.In the Unified Symbol Magic system, every successful spell produces a minimal baseline effect, even if the caster achieves Margin of Success (MoS) 0.Margin of Success represents additional power and manipulation layered on top of this baseline.This rule prevents successful spells from fizzling while ensuring that MoS remains the primary driver of spell scaling.Whenever a spell is successfully cast, it automatically generates the following baseline profile.MoS is spent to increase or modify these values.A caster’s Magery level determines the minimum force their magic can produce.This represents the minimum magical output a caster can achieve with a successful spell.Higher spell power still comes from Margin of Success spending.MoS may be spent to enhance the baseline spell.Common uses include:If a caster rolls MoS 0, the spell still resolves using only the baseline profile.Tessa (Magery 3) casts:Create + FireShe rolls exactly her skill.MoS = 0The spell still produces the baseline effect:2d fire damage Range 10 yards Single targetIf she instead rolled MoS 3, she could upgrade the spell:Damage +2 Range +1Result:4d firebolt 20 yard rangeThis rule ensures that:• Successful spells always produce a meaningful effect • Magery determines baseline magical strength • Margin of Success remains the primary scaling mechanic • Combat spellcasting remains fast and cinematic

item.title: Rule - Casting Time
item.description: Casting time in the Unified Symbol Magic system is determined by the number of Nouns in the spell formula.Each spell always contains one Verb. The number of Nouns determines the spell's complexity and casting time.All spells follow the formula:Verb + 1–3 Nouns Example spells: Create + Fire → Fireball Control + Light → Invisibility Create + Fire + Move → Guided Firebolt Casting time equals the number of nouns in the spell.Example:Create + Fire Casting Time: 1 secondCreate + Fire + Move Casting Time: 2 secondsCreate + Fire + Move + Earth Casting Time: 3 secondsCasting time also limits how much Margin of Success (MoS) can be spent on spell effects.Example (Magery 3 caster):This forces meaningful tactical choices: Fast spells = weaker but immediate Slow spells = stronger but risky in combat "Unlimited MoS" does not bypass Threshold penalties.Casting time only determines how much total MoS may be gathered for the spell. It does not remove the normal Magery limits on how much MoS can be safely spent in a single effect category.Example:Tessa (Magery 3) spends 3 seconds casting a spell and achieves 8 total MoS.She may distribute those MoS across effects freely, but no single category may exceed 3 MoS without triggering the exponential Threshold overage cost.Example allocation:Damage: 3 Area: 2 Range: 2 Duration: 1Legal.Example illegal allocation:Damage: 8The excess MoS beyond Magery applies the double Threshold cost for the overage.This means powerful spells pay two costs:• Time Tax – gathering large MoS pools • Threshold Tax – exceeding safe Magery limitsHighly skilled mages can weave spells faster.Example:A spell with 2-second base casting time becomes 1 second for a skill 20+ caster.This represents elite casters weaving complex symbol chains rapidly.A caster may attempt to rush a spell.Fast Casting Casting time reduced by 1 second Apply –5 penalty to the casting roll Example:A 2-second spell may be cast in 1 second at –5 skill.Failure risks Threshold backlash normally.This system creates meaningful decisions during combat:Casting Time = Number of Nouns MoS Cap = Magery × Seconds Spent Casting Example:Create + Fire 1 second MoS Cap = Magery Create + Fire + Move 2 seconds MoS Cap = Magery × 2

Keep penalties deliberate. item.title: Threshold Magic
item.description: The Core Mechanic No FP Costs: Spells do not cost Fatigue Points (FP) to cast. Instead, they accumulate Threshold (T). Safe Threshold: You can cast safely as long as your accumulated T stays below your campaign's defined Safe Threshold limit. Slow Recovery: Threshold does not reset after every fight. It recovers slowly over time at a fixed rate (e.g., hours or days), making magic an attrition resource during Gate raids. Base Spell Costs Whenever a mage casts a spell, it generates a base amount of Threshold based on its narrative and mechanical weight: The Magery Soft Cap (Overcasting) This is your primary governor on magic scaling: You cannot spend more Margin of Success (MoS) on a single effect category (Damage, Area, Duration, etc.) than your Magery level. The Penalty: You are allowed to exceed this limit, but for every point of MoS spent beyond your Magery cap in a specific category, the Threshold cost for that category doubles exponentially (e.g., 1 over = ×2, 2 over = ×4, 3 over = ×8). Gate Environment Penalties (Mana Pressure) Because Gates are hostile, high-mana environments, simply casting magic inside them is more taxing. Every spell cast incurs a flat Threshold penalty based on the Gate's rank: E-Rank Gate: +0 T D-Rank Gate: +1 T per spell C-Rank Gate: +2 T per spell B-Rank Gate: +3 T per spell A-Rank Gate: +5 T per spell Failure Still Costs If a spell fails, the failure is localized to the spell being cast (it does not cascade to other maintained spells). However, the caster still takes a minimum 1-point Threshold cost for the effort. Magic is tiring even when it misfires. Casting a new spell while maintaining an active spell imposes a –2 penalty to the roll per maintained spell, increasing the chance of this failure. Calamities (Backlash) If a mage's accumulated Threshold exceeds their Safe Limit, they must roll on the Calamity table. Backlash scales by how far over the limit they pushed: Minor: Nosebleeds, severe fatigue, minor spell warping. Moderate: Physical injury, severe backlash, environmental damage. Severe: Unintended summoning, physical mutation, catastrophic Gate reaction (e.g., accelerating a Dungeon Break). The Golden Rule: Use Spent MoS, not Rolled MoS If you base the Threshold on the raw MoS the player rolls, you accidentally punish high-skill mages. If Lena rolls a critical success and gets an MoS of 10, but only wanted to light a campfire, it shouldn't cost her massive Threshold.Instead, the rule must be: Threshold Cost = Total SPENT MoS ÷ 2 (Rounded Up).You only pay for the power you actually inject into the spell. How the Math Looks in Play Because GURPS normally rounds point costs up, dividing by two creates a beautifully smooth, predictable curve: Spend 1–2 MoS (Basic effect) = 1 T Spend 3–4 MoS (Solid combat spell) = 2 T Spend 5–6 MoS (Advanced AOE/Damage) = 3 T Spend 7–8 MoS (Elite power) = 4 T Spend 9–10 MoS (S-Rank devastation) = 5 T The Consequence: Magic Just Got More Efficient In your old system, a "Major/Ultimate" spell cost 7–10 T. Under your new MoS / 2 rule, a massive 10 MoS spell only costs 5 T.This means mages like Lena and Tessa will be able to cast about twice as many spells before risking a Calamity backlash. For a Solo Leveling inspired dungeon-crawl campaign, this is actually a good thing. It gives them the stamina to survive a multi-room C-Rank Gate without needing to take a nap after two fights. How It Connects to Your Existing Rules This new math slots perfectly into the safety governors you've already built: The Magery Soft Cap: You already ruled that spending more MoS in a single category (like Damage) than your Magery level doubles the Threshold cost for the over-cap portion. This stays perfectly intact. (e.g., If Tessa has Magery 3 and spends 5 MoS on Damage, the first 3 MoS are cheap, but the last 2 MoS cost double). Gate Penalties: If they are in a C-Rank Gate (which imposes a +2 T penalty per spell), a 4-MoS fireball costs 2 T (Base) + 2 T (Gate Penalty) = 4 T Total. Failure Cost: You previously established that failing a spell costs a flat 1 T. Under this new math, 1 T is exactly the cost of a minimum-effort spell. This makes logical sense—you burn the equivalent of a basic cantrip just trying to wrestle the mana. Final VerdictChange your rule document to read:"A spell generates Threshold equal to half of the total MoS spent on its effects (rounded up). MoS rolled but not spent generates no Threshold."

item.title: Graymalkin_Academy
item.description: What are all my notes on Graymalkin?Based on our extensive conversations and the provided source material, your notes on Graymalkin Academy have transformed it from a standard D&D 3.5e adventure into a C-to-B Rank transitional Gate tailored perfectly for your GURPS Solo Leveling campaign.Here is the comprehensive summary of your entire Graymalkin Academy conversion: The Core Premise & Backstory Graymalkin is an institutional horror dungeon. It is not a place where monsters invaded; it is a place where a catastrophic system failure occurred. The Catastrophe: Students attempted a high-order summoning experiment that went wrong. Faculty managed to contain the entity in a pentagram, but its essence leaked, poisoning the school with unstable mana and warping the inhabitants. The Theme: The dungeon is a "containment zone that worked too well". The school doesn't want to be saved; it wants to stop happening. Location: The Gate manifests in the real world at William Rainey Harper High School in West Englewood, South Side Chicago. The public cover story is a "hazardous materials incident" and "structural instability" delaying demolition. Layout & Floor Plan (Partial Manifestation) Instead of matching the original two-story-plus-cavern map, the Gate uses "Partial Manifestation" to overlay Graymalkin onto Harper High's structure: Floor 1 (Entry Zone): Warped corridors and staging areas. This is where the Gate physically opens (in the gym or auditorium). Floor 2 (Advanced Classrooms & Labs): Ground zero for magical experiments and defense systems. Floor 3 (Student Dormitories): A new floor added to mimic the feeling of a boarding school. It serves as a claustrophobic, combat-heavy "grinder" filled with mutated students and scavenged loot. Floor 4 (Faculty Quarters & Offices): Elite encounters, where the warped mentors and apex predators reside. The Basement (Magical Boiler Room): Replaces the original Cavern Level. It houses the corrupted mana core/engine that keeps the dungeon alive and leaking mana. The Factions You discarded the D&D diplomatic solutions in favor of a combat-forward approach with four distinct factions locked in a stalemate: The Faculty Remnants (Leftover Stalkers): Tomas and Moira are no longer friendly NPCs. They are corrupted, apex predators ("The Rector-Thing" and "The Pedagogue-Thing") stalking the halls. Their only goal is to attach themselves to a Hunter so they can escape the Gate. The Student Collective: Pack-based, territorial combat groups. They don't negotiate; they use hit-and-run tactics and improvised traps. The Custodial Protocol: The building itself, enforcing obsolete rules via lockdowns, detention fields, and automated constructs. The Containment Failure Wave: You entirely removed the Drow faction. Instead of an outside invasion, the "intruder" monsters are explained as secondary containment breaches and corrupted humanoids native to the disaster. Room-by-Room Bestiary Conversions You replaced generic exotic monsters with thematic, Gate-corrupted enemies: Room 3 (The Balcony): The Homunculus is replaced by The Balcony Reaper, a highly mobile, warped faculty enforcer that drops from the ceiling to ambush PCs. Room 6 (Labs): Xills are replaced by Warped Student Shock Troops (using Orc templates for brutal, pack-based aggression). Room 7 (Elements Lab): Greater Barghests replaced by Disciplined Warped Hobgoblins, representing former senior students fighting in tactical formations. Room 9 (Summoning Chamber): The Succubus is removed. Instead, the room holds the unbroken Pentagram Seal containing the original catastrophe. It is an environmental puzzle—if broken, it unleashes a massive mana explosion and an entity escapes into Chicago. Room 10 (Herbarium): Grimlocks replaced by Arcane-Burned Enforcers, blinded students who track heartbeats and mana. Room 12 (Door Guard): The Shield Guardian is now the Graymalkin Internal Defense Unit (G-IDU), an automated construct that misidentifies all living beings as hostile non-students. Room 18 (Trophy Hall): Gibbering Mouther replaced by the Corrupted Mana Ooze, a psychological terror for mages that feeds on and punishes spellcasting. Room 20 (Dorms): Zombie Ogres replaced by Drow-Altered Ogres (or Dormitory Brutes), serving as massive living shock troops. Room 22 (Mess Hall): Gray Render replaced by a Corrupted Stone Giant / Ogre Titan, a student/groundskeeper swollen by ambient mana. Room 25 (Classroom): The Ghouls remain but are converted to Gate-Touched Ghouls. They are ambush predators posing as corpses, designed to drain resources via paralysis. Room 29 (Headmaster's Office): The Rakshasa boss is replaced by The Corrupted Headmaster, a spell-matrix entity that enforces institutional order through lethal "directives" and environmental control. Loot & Vault Mechanics The Vault: You removed the cavern vault. The "Vault" is now an abstract spell-state or distributed system (like the Headmaster's Archive) protected by administrative authority, not rock. Monster Drops: All living, mana-sustained beings (like the Student Shock Troops) dissolve when killed, leaving behind Monster Cores. Scavenged Loot: Since the cavern level was removed, the treasure those monsters originally hoarded has been dragged upstairs into dorm lockers and classrooms—damaged, trapped, and mixed with mundane school supplies.

item.title: Example_Session
item.description: Primary Tone: Economic & Moral Tension Secondary Tone: Subtle Oversight Pressure Team cleared Fire Opal Gate (C-Rank). Encountered unexpected A-Rank vampire mini-boss. Fight was long and resource-draining. Ryan burned Luck to survive final exchange. Lena and Tessa expended most magical reserves. One hunter was rescued earlier (insanity case). Gate collapsed successfully. Loot recovered including 1 A-Core (vampire), 3 B, 3 C, 9 E, 3 F, 3 bone devil stingers. Tessa evaluates whether to pocket high-grade core. Ryan calculates legal vs black market payout. Lena remains neutral but observant. Possible internal debate about legality. Possible discreet contact with black market broker. DPS Field Agent Morales – Processing Officer Motivation: Maintain procedure, avoid paperwork spikes.DPS Tech Halpern – Core Scanner Motivation: Do job efficiently, mildly curious about A-core.Rescued Hunter (Derrick Vale) – Psychological Casualty Motivation: Shaken, fragmented memory, not reliable witness.Tier 2 Broker (Potential): “Mr. Alder” Motivation: Expand client base, interested in undead cores.Underworld Standing: 0 DPS Suspicion: 0 Possible Buyer Tier: Tier 2 Broker Complication Trigger: Buyer requests exclusivity if A-core shown.Audit Risk: Low (no drone telemetry) Attitude Toward Team: Respectful but cautious Recent Flags: Unexpected spike anomaly logged. Fire Opal classification marked “C-Rank with A-tier variance.” DPS agent remarks: “Didn’t expect that kind of density in a C-site.” Tech scanner lingers slightly longer on A-core. Ryan privately calculates: $120,000 legal payout. Tessa notices no precise count recorded for C-cores. Derrick mutters: “It wasn’t normal… that thing wasn’t C…” Tessa pockets 1 C-core during inventory shuffle. Broker meeting arranged in South Loop warehouse. Broker reacts strongly to vampire resonance. Offers 20% above baseline if exclusivity agreed. Silent enforcer present in room. (To move into permanent files) Fire Opal officially classified as “C-Rank with Spike Event.” DPS Trust remains neutral. Underworld Standing +1 if sale successful. DPS Suspicion +1 if core count discrepancy later noted. Mr. Alder added to Black Market NPC list.

item.title: 🎲 BLACK MARKET ENCOUNTER GENERATOR
item.description: Use this generator when: A Hunter attempts to sell cores illegally. A broker must be introduced quickly. A deal feels too smooth. You need tension without combat. You want structured Social Engineering play. This tool supports fast improvisation during live sessions.Roll 1d6 or choose.1 – Street Fence (Tier 1) Nervous, opportunistic. Slightly overpays to hook new sellers. High betrayal risk. Possibly flipped by DPS. 2 – Independent Broker (Tier 2) Professional and calm. Tests authenticity carefully. Interested in repeat business. Mid-level criminal connections. 3 – Syndicate Representative (Tier 3) Polite but quiet. Silent security nearby. Evaluates the sellers more than the core. May offer exclusivity. 4 – Academic Middleman Claims research purpose. Too clean. Possibly DPS-adjacent or cult-adjacent. Asks technical questions. 5 – Rival Hunter Moving Cores Recognizes the PCs. Competitive. May attempt partnership or undercut. Could become recurring contact. 6 – Unexpected Third Party Gang lieutenant interrupts. Scanner chatter nearby. Power flickers. Someone else is watching. Roll 1d6.1 – Pure Profit Wants margin. Nothing personal.2 – Territory Enforcement Testing whether PCs respect boundaries.3 – Information Gathering Asks too many questions about Fire Opal.4 – Recruitment Angle Hints at larger operations.5 – Ritual Demand Specifically interested in undead/demon cores.6 – Political Leverage Interested in Ryan’s family or public visibility.Roll secretly if tension is needed.1 – Heat Someone nearby recognizes the PCs.2 – Underpayment Attempt Buyer claims core is mana-scarred (-20%).3 – Exclusivity Demand Higher price offered in exchange for loyalty.4 – Territory Conflict “This corridor isn’t yours.”5 – Core Resonance A-core pulses or reacts unexpectedly.6 – Clean No complication. Smooth deal.Use these if running structured Social Engineering.Finding a Buyer: Streetwise (IQ-based) Negotiation: Merchant vs Merchant or Fast-Talk vs Merchant Lying About Grade: Fast-Talk vs Merchant Spotting Deception: Merchant or Detect Lies Intimidation: Intimidation vs Will Reaction Roll modifies: Offer price Respect level Future access Base Black Market Price × Modifier:Poor Reaction: ×0.75 Neutral Reaction: ×1.0 Good Reaction: ×1.25 Very Good Reaction: ×1.5 Critical Success: Add Favor opportunity. Critical Failure: PCs marked unreliable. Drop one in instantly.Warehouse Fluorescent flicker. Pallets. Smell of ozone.Basement Poker Room Music overhead. Green banker’s lamp. Guard at door.Restaurant Back Room Plastic tablecloth. Bodyguard silent in corner.Abandoned CTA Tunnel Portable generator hum. Metal briefcase exchange.Track two hidden values:Underworld Standing: -3 to +3 DPS Suspicion: 0 to 5 Each illegal sale: +1 Underworld Standing +1 DPS Suspicion (if sloppy or large transaction)At Suspicion 3: Audit triggered. At Suspicion 5: Investigation arc begins. Because the team cleared a spike dungeon:Selling: C-Core → Routine tension. B-Core → Serious buyer interest. A-Core → Tier 3 involvement guaranteed. Do not escalate to crackdown immediately. Let tension build gradually. Do not punish first offense instantly. Escalate consequences slowly. Criminal consequences are personal, not legal. Reputation spreads slowly. A-Rank cores are political events. Money is powerful; leverage is stronger. Always leave room for retreat.

item.title: GM_Guidelines
item.description: These guidelines govern how the Chicago criminal underworld behaves in play.The goal is tension, not punishment. The goal is pressure, not shutdown.Hunters skimming small amounts is common.First-time illegal sales should: Succeed Feel dangerous Leave lingering uncertainty Immediate catastrophic consequences discourage interesting choices.Illegal behavior should trigger:1st instance → Clean sale 2nd instance → Broker curiosity 3rd instance → Territorial friction 4th instance → Surveillance / pressure 5th instance → Enforcement or leverage Escalation should feel organic.The underworld does not: Call police File reports Issue warnings They: Cut access Demand repayment Enforce territory Apply pressure quietly DPS consequences are bureaucratic. Criminal consequences are immediate and personal.Underworld Standing should move between -3 to +3.Reputation changes: After major deals After betrayals After territory violations After exclusivity agreements Do not swing reputation wildly without clear cause.A-core transactions: Always involve Tier 3 buyers Always create memory in the network May create future leverage They should never feel routine.Cash is temporary.Favors, exclusivity agreements, and obligations create: Long-term hooks Story momentum Moral tension Encourage brokers to offer: "I can do better, if you owe me."Brokers are: Smart Connected Experienced They are not: Psychic All-seeing Automatically aware of every lie Use Reaction Rolls and Influence Contests. Do not pre-decide outcomes.Treat negotiations like combat: Stakes defined Skills matter Margin of success matters Long-term consequences tracked This is Social Engineering in action.Do not force corruption. Do not force compliance.Present: Temptation Risk Opportunity Let them choose.The world reacts accordingly.Even if they overstep: Give warning signs Give negotiation options Give social escape routes Campaign tension thrives on choices, not traps.

item.title: Social_Engineering_Chicago_Underworld
item.description: This document adapts GURPS Social Engineering (4e) to the criminal underworld economy surrounding Monster Cores in Chicago.This is not a corporate shadow economy.This is a criminal network built on: Territory Reputation Violence Debt Silence Risk management The Subterranean Market operates beneath the official Hunter economy and outside DPS oversight. Do not bring heat. Do not misrepresent grade. Do not short the house. Respect territorial control. Favors are remembered longer than money. Breaking these rules results in: Loss of access Forced partnerships Violence Being quietly removed from the network

item.title: Running_Social_Conflict

Tier 2 brokers are cautious. Tier 3 syndicates are politically shielded.Hunters operating illegally risk: Increased audit scrutiny Assignment restrictions Suspended licensing Quiet surveillance Criminal consequences are social and violent. item.title: Symbolism & Doctrine
item.description: A fractured circle intersected by three descending lines.Interpretation: The circle = dimensional boundary. The fractures = breach. The lines = descent of the Archmage. Members often wear this subtly: Pendants Rings Tattoo fragments They believe: The collapse was a necessary purification stage.Reality: It was catastrophic disruption.They believe: Tessa must realize her destiny.Reality: She is not his vessel.This is accidentally correct.Their rituals and devotion are stabilizing Koga Thun’s echo.They believe worship empowers him.In truth: It prevents dissipation. Dream incubation circles. Symbol carving at minor Gate sites. Blood-binding oaths. Astral alignment meditations. Attempted Gate harmonization. Most rituals are symbolic.A few actually resonate.There is growing fracture within the Cult:Faction A: “Prepare the Vessel.”Faction B: “Find a Better Host.”Faction C: “Stabilize the Archmage without incarnation.”This ideological split can destabilize them from within.

item.title: Suspected Financial Backers

They believe in survival beyond death.There are signs of: Anonymous cryptocurrency infusions. Purchases of obscure arcane texts. Artifact acquisition from European black markets. Possibility: A Greyhawk-aligned actor is seeding funds.Unconfirmed.

item.title: Overview
item.description: Esoteric Revivalist Cult Primary Activity: Ritual convergence, symbolic alignment, vessel identification Operational Area: Chicago (Primary), scattered online cellsThe Cult believes: Koga Thun is a transcendent archmage destined to cross worlds. The Fall 2024 breach was a prophesied event. The Gate collapse was not failure, but interruption. Tessa is the intended Avatar. His return requires preparation and purification. They are wrong about the Avatar.They are correct that he still exists.The Cult is not centralized.It consists of: Core Inner Circle (ritual practitioners) Devoted Believers (active members) Online Sympathizers Financial Backers Fringe Conspiracy Amplifiers Most members do not understand actual dimensional mechanics.Only a handful perform true ritual work. Reconstruct the breach sequence. Identify the “True Vessel.” Locate or create stable Gate sites. Gather relics tied to Greyhawk cosmology. Protect Tessa from “corruption” or federal interference. They believe they are preparing the world for ascension.In reality, they are stabilizing a fading echo.Individually: low to moderate threat. Collectively: potentially catastrophic if ritual convergence aligns with a major Gate event.The Cult is more dangerous for what they might attempt than what they currently can achieve.

item.title: Koga Thun
item.description: Multiversal Archmage (Diminished Echo State – Modern World)Prime Dimension: Greyhawk Status in Greyhawk: Living (Peak Power) Status in Modern World: Disembodied Arcane EchoKoga Thun is not a god.He is a powerful mortal archmage from the Greyhawk dimension who sought transcendence through interplanar breach. His goal was not conquest, but survival and expansion — to escape the limitations of a single world and establish influence across realities.In Fall 2024, he attempted to cross into the Modern World using an artificial Gate constructed by Malcolm Lockwood’s resources and ritual knowledge.The crossing failed.He was severed mid-transition and shunted back into the Modern World without a host.He now exists as a diminished metaphysical echo. Artificial Gate constructed at Chicago college basement. Dimensional alignment achieved temporarily. Tessa identified by Koga Thun as optimal vessel candidate. Essence transfer initiated. Gate destroyed before full reformation. Koga Thun's projection destabilized. Essence violently ejected into Modern dimension. No physical manifestation achieved. Result: He cannot reform without a compatible anchor.Koga Thun exists as: A fragmented arcane pattern. A consciousness without a body. A diminished but self-aware entity. Dependent on belief to maintain coherence. He cannot: Manifest physically. Possess unwilling hosts. Directly control Gates. Exert large-scale magical force. He can: Whisper into dreams of receptive minds. Influence ritual resonance if aligned properly. Subtly nudge emotionally unstable followers. Persist through cult belief. Without followers, he would gradually dissipate.Belief does not increase his power — it stabilizes his existence.The cult believes: Tessa is his Avatar. The failed breach was prophecy. His weakening was part of ascension. His return is inevitable. They are wrong.Tessa was a target, not a vessel. Compatibility was miscalculated. The transfer never completed.The cult misinterprets survival as incarnation.They function as a psychic anchor network, unknowingly preventing his dissolution. Full archmage capacity. True body. Ritual mastery. Political and arcane influence. No body. No host. Cannot independently reform. Limited to psychic bleed-through. He is significantly weaker in the Modern World than in Greyhawk.Koga Thun believed Tessa was an ideal vessel during the breach due to: Psychological instability. Magical compatibility signature. Metaphysical receptivity. He was wrong.The overwrite never occurred. She is not possessed. She is not his avatar. She carries no fragment of his essence.However: Her survival during the breach created cult fixation.Whether Koga Thun still considers her viable is unresolved.None directly.Lena’s splintered sorcerer-queen power is unrelated to Koga Thun’s lineage. Her arcane vector is older and independent.There is no inherent alignment or opposition unless developed through play.Indirect.Ryan’s father enabled the breach.Koga Thun viewed Malcolm Lockwood as a tool, not a partner.Ryan holds no metaphysical relevance to Koga Thun.His importance is political, not arcane.To reform in the Modern World, Koga Thun would require: A stabilized Gate of sufficient duration. A metaphysically compatible host. Ritual alignment across dimensions. Significant cult amplification. Without all four, manifestation fails.Koga Thun should function as: A destabilizing background presence. A whispering myth. A cult catalyst. A shadow of former ambition. He should not: Become the immediate main villain. Override player agency. Escalate automatically with Gate activity. Behave as an omniscient entity. His influence grows only if intentionally amplified.Koga Thun is closer to: A wounded Vecna before godhood. A Thulsa Doom without an empire. A brilliant mage who miscalculated. He is dangerous because of ambition, not divinity.You may escalate him by: Increasing cult organization. Allowing dream communication clarity. Introducing relics from Greyhawk. Creating ritual convergence events. Or diminish him by: Cult fragmentation. Failed rituals. Loss of belief coherence. Exposure of fraud within cult ranks. Koga Thun failed.He knows he failed.He survives not because he is destined — but because others refuse to let him fade.

item.title: LOC - Calumet Ruins
item.description:
Think steel mills, slag heaps, rail yards, river pollution, and forgotten infrastructure. Calumet is where Gates don’t hide — they fester.Use six zones here. Calumet is larger, messier, and more openly hostile than Englewood.(Primary Gate Cluster)Map Marking Dark red fill Gear / flame icons Jagged borders What This Is Former steel mill complexes Blast furnaces and rolling mills The first Calumet Gate opened inside a furnace hall Rules Impact Extreme heat pockets Fire-aligned mana −1 FP every 30 minutes without protection Fire/metal monsters are territorial and aggressive Notes Multiple Gates opened here over time Some sealed, some dormant This is where Fire Opal–type Gates are more likely (Environmental Death Zone)Map Marking Orange-black mottled fill Toxic / collapse icons What This Is Mountains of industrial waste Sinkholes Toxic runoff Cracked ground venting heat and gas Rules Impact HT checks vs toxins Movement penalties Random environmental damage Monsters burrow and ambush Notes Looks inert until it isn’t Government pretends this is an EPA issue (Monster Transit Zone)Map Marking Yellow dashed outline Train / tunnel icons What This Is Abandoned rail lines Switching yards Collapsed maintenance tunnels Rules Impact High encounter frequency Monsters use rails like highways Easy ambushes Loud combat attracts reinforcements Notes Hunters hate this zone Cultists use it to move cores (Aquatic Hazard Zone)Map Marking Purple-blue shading Water / biohazard icons What This Is Polluted river sections Flooded industrial basements Submerged tunnels Rules Impact Waterborne monsters Disease checks Visibility penalties Unstable footing Notes Some Gates open partially underwater Creatures migrate upstream at night (Unofficial Control Zone)Map Marking Green outline Wrench / crate icons What This Is Warehouses and yards used by hunters Temporary camps Core processing sites Rules Impact Easier resupply Faster extraction Increased chance of hunter NPCs Guild influence is visible here Notes This zone exists because Calumet produces valuable cores Conflicts happen, but quietly (Hidden Subsurface Layer)Map Marking Black dashed overlay Utility icons What This Is Power conduits Cooling tunnels Drainage systems Old bomb shelters Rules Impact Navigation penalties Monsters appear where they shouldn’t Gates can “bleed” between zones Notes This is how Calumet connects to Englewood’s subterranean spill The two zones talk to each other Calumet is where the government lets things get ugly, because it’s easier to justify. South-southeast of Englewood Follow the Calumet River Wrap zones around: old steel mills rail corridors industrial dead space Overlay order (top → bottom): C-6 Black Infrastructure C-4 River C-1 Furnace Core C-2 Slag Fields C-3 Rail Graveyard C-5 Hunter Strip It’s where Fire Opal–class threats aren’t rare It produces high-value cores It attracts: cultists corporations reckless hunters It connects underground to Englewood If Englewood is a warning…Calumet is exploitation.What is the history of Calumet?Here’s a grounded, Chicago-real history of the Calumet area, tuned so it naturally explains why it became a Gate magnet instead of feeling like “because magic.”

4A place that was never meant to be quiet again.Long before furnaces and rail yards, the Calumet region was: marshland slow water liminal ground between lake, river, and land Indigenous peoples avoided permanent settlement here. Not for superstition—because the ground shifted, flooded, swallowed structures.Even then, it was a place that didn’t like being owned.Chicago’s south industrial expansion turned Calumet into a machine.Steel mills, coke ovens, rail yards, and ship canals were packed together because: water access rail access political indifference to pollution What that created: constant vibration extreme heat gradients chemical runoff buried infrastructure layered on buried infrastructure Calumet wasn’t just polluted. It was mechanically stressed for a century.Steel collapsed. Industry fled.What stayed behind: sealed tunnels abandoned furnaces slag heaps undocumented voids contaminated groundwater rusting machines still under tension The land didn’t recover. It hollowed out.By the 1990s, Calumet was already: semi-forgotten politically convenient to ignore dangerous in mundane ways Which made it perfect later.For decades, Calumet existed as: “future redevelopment land” EPA problem zones rail corridors no one wanted to map fully Nothing supernatural—just: sinkholes unexplained fires toxic gas releases structural collapses But here’s the key part for your setting: Calumet already behaved like a place where reality leaked. So when Gates began appearing globally…It didn’t open in a neighborhood.It opened inside: a sealed furnace hall surrounded by slag beneath rusted catwalks above flooded tunnels Sensors didn’t notice immediately. Cameras didn’t work right. Heat signatures blended with the environment.By the time anyone understood what had happened: monsters had space to spread mana had room to pool no civilians were present to trigger alarms The government’s internal conclusion was chilling: “If a Gate had to open somewhere, this was the least bad place.” That decision shaped everything.In-world logic, not GM fiat: The ground is fractured and hollow Old infrastructure forms natural containment chambers Heat and pressure align with fire- and metal-aligned Gates Subterranean networks allow migration Political will to fully cleanse the area is low Calumet isn’t cursed.It’s convenient.Today, Calumet is: semi-abandoned semi-monitored quietly exploited It’s where: dangerous Gates are allowed to fester high-value - monster cores are harvested experimental containment is tested failures are buried Englewood taught the city a lesson.Calumet is where that lesson is applied.Among hunters, Calumet is known as: “The Furnace” “The Open Wound” “Where the city bleeds money” You don’t go there to survive. You go there to get paid.And maybe not come back.This lets you: justify recurring Gates without escalation fatigue explain government tolerance seed corporate and cult interest tie Fire Opal–style threats naturally to the region contrast Englewood’s tragedy with Calumet’s exploitation Englewood was an accident.Calumet is a choice.

item.title: RULE - Campaign Constitution
item.description: This document defines the non-negotiable mechanical foundations of the campaign. If a rule is not stated here, it is either: An optional expansion A GM ruling A derived consequence of these rules When in doubt, this document overrides all others.The campaign uses GURPS 4th Edition as its mechanical base.The following books are considered rules-valid sources: GURPS Basic Set (Characters & Campaigns) GURPS Magic GURPS Thaumatology GURPS High-Tech GURPS Dungeon Fantasy (select material) GURPS Monster Hunters (select material) Rules from these books apply only where not superseded by this manifest. Characters are cinematic but mortal Combat is fast, decisive, and dangerous Magic is powerful, flexible, and risky The game assumes competent protagonists, not average civilians Optional cinematic rules may be used at the GM’s discretion, but core mechanics remain grounded in GURPS resolution. Characters may Move and Attack in the same turn without penalty, unless performing: All-Out Attacks All-Out Defenses This rule applies equally to PCs and NPCs Retreats, defenses, and active reactions function normally This replaces standard GURPS movement/attack limitations.All rolls use standard 3d6 roll-under mechanics. Margin of Success (MoS) is always calculated Margin of Failure (MoF) matters when relevant When multiple skills are rolled for a single action, the lowest MoS is used Critical successes and failures follow Basic Set rules unless explicitly overridden.Magic does not use fixed spell lists.All magic is constructed using Symbols, divided into:Create, Move, Control, Sense, Heal, Protect, WeakenAir, Water, Fire, Earth, Body, Mind, Light, Sound, Plant, Animal, Necromancy, Knowledge, Meta-MagicA spell consists of: 1 Verb 1–3 Nouns Example: Create + Fire → Fireball Control + Light → Invisibility To cast a spell: Roll lowest involved Symbol skill Determine MoS for each roll MoS determines the spell’s strength and scaling If any required roll fails, the spell fails. Magery governs: Maximum complexity of spells Maximum MoS spent per effect category A character may not spend more MoS on a single effect category than their Magery level Excess MoS may still be used, but increases magical risk (see Threshold Magic) Magic uses Threshold Magic, not fatigue-based costs. Each spell adds Threshold (T) instead of FP cost Threshold recovers over time at a fixed rate Exceeding Threshold risks Calamities Minor spells: 1–3 T Moderate spells: 4–6 T Major / Ultimate spells: 7–10+ T Calamities are magical, narrative, and potentially severe. Maintaining a spell is passive Casting a new spell while maintaining one imposes a –2 penalty per maintained spell Failure affects only the newly cast spell unless Threshold backlash occurs Damage uses standard GURPS damage types and DR Area effects, homing effects, control effects, etc. are determined by MoS allocation Magic may create effects that mimic Advantages, Attacks, or Conditions, but does not grant permanent traits unless explicitly allowed Technology Level is modern (TL8 baseline unless stated otherwise) Equipment legality, black markets, and scarcity are enforced Modern weapons are lethal; armor matters Technomagical items exist but are rare and controlled Monsters are ecological entities, not XP bundles Stat blocks emphasize: Behavior Ecology Tactics Monsters may retreat, negotiate, or act irrationally Not all encounters are balanced or fair Character advancement is point-based Advancement may occur through: Training Study Story milestones Exceptional play Power growth is intentional but controlled The GM: Interprets MoS outcomes Defines narrative consequences Adjudicates edge cases However, the GM does not override core mechanics without explicitly declaring a house rule.This document does three crucial things: It locks physics before lore It separates rules from rulings It gives players confidence that mastery is possible Next logical steps (when you’re ready): A Magic Allocation Cheat Sheet (MoS → Damage / Area / Control) A Combat Reference Card for modern + magic interaction A “GM Only” Design Appendix explaining why these rules exist (kept out of player view) When you want, we can tighten this further for table print, or build the next layer without contaminating the core.should each section be its own note? like should 1. System Baseline have its own note?Short answer first, because clarity beats ceremony:No — not at first. The Core Rules Manifest should remain one single note.Now the longer, more interesting answer: why that’s true, and when it stops being true.A constitution is powerful precisely because it’s hard to fragment.Your Core Rules Manifest is not a reference manual. It’s a statement of reality. The moment you split it into multiple notes, three bad things start happening: Authority diffuses Players (and future-you) start asking “Which note overrides which?” Drift sneaks in One section gets quietly updated, another doesn’t. Congratulations — you’ve invented accidental edition wars. Obsidian starts lying Links make everything look equally important, even when it isn’t. A constitution lives or dies by coherence. One file forces coherence.Right now, your manifest should be: One document that can be printed, handed to a player, and sworn upon. If you cannot print it as a single artifact without losing meaning, it’s too fragmented.There is a correct time to split — just not yet.You split only when a section gains subordinate structure.Here’s the rule of thumb: A section becomes its own note only when it needs children. Let’s apply that to your examples.1. System Baseline This is declarative. It names books and authority. It has no moving parts.If it were its own note, you’d gain nothing and risk someone “editing the foundation.”Same for: Tone and Power Assumptions Action Economy GM Authority Clause These are axioms, not systems.Unified Symbol Magic SystemRight now, it belongs in the manifest as a law. Later, it will absolutely spawn: Magic Allocation Tables Example Spells Edge Cases Design Rationale Player vs GM guidance When that happens, the manifest keeps the summary, and a separate document becomes: “Unified Symbol Magic — Full Rules” The manifest links outward, but never imports detail inward.These will eventually want their own notes: Monsters (already happening naturally) Equipment economies Advancement rules Faction mechanics Dungeon / Gate rules But note the pattern: Those are procedural systems, not constitutional laws.Here’s the rule that prevents vault collapse: Top-level documents never link sideways. They only link downward. Your Core Rules Manifest should: Sit at the root Have no backlinks that alter it Be referenced, not edited casually Everything else orbits it.For now, I’d suggest:00 - CORE RULES MANIFEST.md 01 - Magic System (Expansion).md 02 - Combat & Damage Clarifications.md 03 - Monsters & Ecology.md 04 - Equipment & Economy.md GM - Design Notes (Private).mdNotice: The manifest stays singular Expansions explain, but do not redefine GM notes are quarantined Fragmentation feels productive. Coherence is productive.You’ve already done the hard work: designing a system that hangs together. The manifest’s job is to freeze that coherence.Once the ice is solid, then you can build cities on top of it.Next time, if you want, we can: Mark which sentences in the manifest are link anchors Decide which sections are immutable vs versioned Or design a “Player Cut” vs “GM Cut” without duplicating rules You’re building this the right way.

item.title: Task Difficulty
item.description: Difficulty Modifiers are separate from personal modifiers (culture, equipment, tech level). They apply to the task itself and affect anyone attempting it.Rule of Thumb: These modifiers assume a trained character. If a character is using a Default, add the default penalty to these modifiers (e.g., a +5 "Easy" task becomes "Average" for someone at a -5 Default). Cumulative: These stack with personal modifiers (Voice, Language, etc.). The "Fast" Rule: If the action is too fast to calculate every tiny modifier (like a car in bad repair), simply bump the Difficulty Level up or down by 1–2 steps instead of hunting for specific equipment penalties.

item.title: GURPS_Solo_Leveling_Campaign_Plan
item.description: Campaign Name: GURPS: Solo Leveling – Gate CrisisSystem: GURPS 4th Edition (Modern / Action / Dungeon Fantasy hybrid)Primary Inspirations: Solo Leveling Modern dungeon raiding Monster Hunters D&D dungeon modules adapted to GURPS Tone & Style: Modern urban fantasy Dangerous, lethal dungeons Gradual power escalation Tactical combat with cinematic flair Mystery surrounding the origin of Gates Gates began appearing across the modern world without warning. Each Gate leads to an enclosed extradimensional dungeon filled with hostile creatures and supernatural phenomena.Hunters — individuals with exceptional combat skill or magical aptitude — are licensed to enter Gates, clear them, and retrieve valuable artifacts.If a Gate is not cleared in time, it risks a Dungeon Break, releasing monsters into the real world.Base TL: TL8 (Modern Day)Inside Gates: Technology works normally Electronics may glitch or fail at GM discretion Mana presence interferes with precision sensors Hunter Gear: Firearms, armor, drones, explosives Limited-use technomagical gear Adept-compatible rune items Gates are self-contained environments Monsters do not retreat outside the Gate unless a break occurs Clearing the boss collapses the Gate Time distortion is possible (GM tool) Advancement Style: Points awarded after Gate clears Milestone bonuses for bosses and discoveries Rare advantages unlocked via artifacts or awakening Spell Formula: Verb + 1–3 NounsVerbs: Create, Move, Control, Sense, Heal, Protect, WeakenNouns: Air, Animal, Body, Earth, Fire, Plant, Sound, Water, Light, Necromancy, Mind, Knowledge, Meta-MagicResolution: Roll all involved skills Lowest Margin of Success determines effect strength Threshold Magic governs risk and backlash No Magery Use weapons, tactics, and gear Can use Adept or rune-based items Limited supernatural abilities Minor noun/verb effects Emergency or support magic Full access to Symbol Magic High risk, high reward Vulnerable without protection Design Philosophy: Converted from D&D, rebuilt for GURPS logic Fewer spell-like abilities, more thematic powers Gate-Touched Template adds: Increased durability Unnatural resilience Mana-based traits Primary Sources: Monstrous Compendium (Enraged Eggplant) Mage Items Enhance spellcasting Threshold modifiers Mana storage Adept Items Rune magic Single-use or cooldown effects Technomagical Gear Firearms with mana effects Armor with resistances Sensors attuned to Gates Licenses hunters Assigns Gate rankings Covers up civilian exposure Competing interests Corporate-sponsored teams Black-market artifact trade Power imbalance between ranks Moral cost of hunting Secrets behind the Gates What happens when Hunters become monsters? Gate overlays for FoundryVTT Rank-based encounter scaling Dungeon templates by Gate rank Optional cinematic rules enabled

item.title: Core_Value_Table
item.description: 1. The Graded Pricing System (Government vs. Black Market) In your GURPS Solo Leveling Conversion notes, you established a base system tied to the monster's threat level, with different rates depending on who the hunters sell to:• Government Buyback Rates (Legal): This is what the Department of Paranormal Security (DPS) or Hunter Registry officially pays.    ◦ F-Grade: $50    ◦ E-Grade: $200    ◦ D-Grade: $800    ◦ C-Grade: $3,500    ◦ B-Grade: $18,000    ◦ A-Grade: $120,000    ◦ S-Grade: $850,000+• Black Market Pricing (The Subterranean Market): Illegal buyers generally pay 3x the government rate, scaling up to 10x if the core is exceedingly rare, intact, or "fresh".    ◦ F-Grade: $150    ◦ E-Grade: $600    ◦ D-Grade: $2,400    ◦ C-Grade: $10,500    ◦ B-Grade: $54,000    ◦ A-Grade: $400,000    ◦ S-Grade: $3,000,000+2. The Dungeon-Level Payout System In your GURPS Solo Leveling - Selling Monster Cores document, you also outlined a broader "per intact core" pricing structure based on the rank of the dungeon they were extracted from (specifically referencing the Fire Opal dungeon).• E-Rank Dungeon: 1,000–3,000 per core• D-Rank Dungeon: 5,000–15,000 per core• C-Rank Dungeon (like Fire Opal): 25,000–60,000 per core3. Condition and Boss Modifiers Your notes also include specific rules for how the condition of the core affects its final sale price:• Boss Cores: Worth 2x to 4x the normal value.• Cracked Cores: Suffer a -50% value penalty.• Mana-Scarred Core (from gate collapses): Suffer a -20% value penalty unless the buyer specifically wants instability.

item.title: Mana-Scarred Core
item.description: a mana-scarred core is a monster core that was extracted right as a Gate violently collapsed.When a dungeon boss is killed and the Gate closes, it shuts "like a guillotine on reality itself," releasing a massive pressure wave of dust, heat, and mana. Cores that are inside the dungeon during this collapse absorb some of that chaotic energy, leaving them "mana-scarred".Here is what that means practically in your campaign:• Trace Instability: These cores are physically and magically altered. For example, cores from the Fire Opal dungeon collapse are warm to the touch, faintly glowing, and highly volatile if damaged (meaning you shouldn't keep them next to explosives).• A Penalty to Value: Because they are unstable, mana-scarred cores generally suffer a -20% value penalty when sold to standard buyers (like the government or standard Guild merchants) who prefer safe, pristine cores.• A Unique Black-Market Asset: While normal buyers dock their pay, specific buyers want that instability. Defense contractors, arcane researchers, and enchantment houses specializing in destructive gear or anti-monster incendiaries will actively seek out these volatile cores for their explosive properties.• High Risk: If the players hold onto them instead of selling them, they can be used to fuel powerful, one-off enchantments, but they can also become dangerous liabilities if they destabilize in the party's inventory.In short, a mana-scarred core is a flawed but highly explosive power source that proves the hunters barely escaped a collapsing dungeon.

item.title: Vision, Light & Torches
item.description: EQUIPMENTTorch - A torch burns for 1 hour, providing bright light in a 20-foot radius and dim light for an additional 20 feet. If you make a melee attack with a burning torch and hit, it deals 1 fire damage.Lantern, Bullseye - A bullseye lantern casts bright light in a 60-foot cone and dim light for an additional 60 feet. Once lit, it burns for 6 hours on a flask (1 pint) of oil.Lantern, Hooded - A hooded lantern casts bright light in a 30-foot radius and dim light for an additional 30 feet. Once lit, it burns for 6 hours on a flask (1 pint) of oil. As an action, you can lower the hood, reducing the light to dim light in a 5-foot radius.Candle - For 1 hour, a candle sheds bright light in a 5-foot radius and dim light for an additional 5 feet.

item.title: Chicago_Operations
item.description:
Status: High Alert / Unstable Focus: LOC - O'Hare Containment Zone & LOC - Navy Pier GateChicago is considered a "Hot Zone" due to the high density of dimensional stress fractures. Response Time: Faster than national average. QRF (Quick Reaction Force) can reach downtown in 15 minutes via helicopter from O'Hare. The Subterranean Market: The Chicago Cell tolerates the market beneath the city because it acts as a pressure valve and information source. They do not raid it as long as violence stays underground.
Englewood: Used as a training ground and punishment detail. "Buffer duty" in LOC - Englewood is a common assignment for hunters who break protocol.

item.title: Operational_Doctrine
item.description:
The priority is never exploration; it is preventing a Breach. If a Gate cannot be cleared, it must be sealed. If it cannot be sealed, the surrounding area is condemned (e.g., LOC - Englewood).
Harvesting: All Monster_Cores must be harvested to prevent mana saturation. Turn-In: Cores must be sold to authorized Federal buyers or licensed brokers. Hoarding high-level cores is considered "possession of unregulated nuclear material."
Black Market: Selling to the Subterranean_Market is illegal but rampant. The ARD looks the other way for small amounts, but cracks down on bulk smuggling. Due to the Koga Thun Resonance (classified), modern technology degrades inside Chicago Gates. Rank D/E: Minor static. Rank C: Complex electronics fail (-1 penalty). Rank B: Drones and smart-optics unreliable (-2 penalty). Rank A: Analog tech required. Electronics dead. Doctrine: Hunters are advised to carry mechanical backups (revolvers, pump shotguns, blades) for high-rank incursions. Mixed-unit tactics are mandated for high-level raids. Awakened (Mages): Provide artillery and shield support. Adepts: Provide rune-utility and emergency stabilization. Mundane: Provide kinetic volume of fire and tactical flexibility.

item.title: Rank_Structure
item.description: The "S through E" ranking system is used internationally, but the DHS uses specific pay-grade titles for contractors. Description: Entry-level contractors, often expendable or in training. Clearance: Low. Need-to-know only. Gear: Standard civilian firearms allowed. No heavy weaponry. Privileges: Access to the Subterranean Market is tolerated but not officially sanctioned. Description: Proven professionals. The backbone of the division. Clearance: Moderate. Can view briefing dossiers on local Gates. Gear: Access to restricted ammo (AP/Silver). Privileges: Federal Concealed Carry permit. Access to Guild medical facilities. Description: Elite assets. Often lead raid teams. Clearance: High. Aware of Gate instability metrics. Gear: Authorization for heavy ordnance (explosives, anti-materiel) inside containment zones. Privileges: Can request Emergency Extraction Teams (QRF). Direct line to Federal Liaisons. Description: Strategic assets. Often assigned to single high-threat Gates (like LOC - Navy Pier Gate). Clearance: Top Secret/Anomalous. Privileges: Can commandeer local resources. Political immunity. Description: Nation-state level power. Status: Closely monitored by the DoD. Often viewed as potential threats rather than employees.

item.title: Legal_Status
item.description: Hunters operate in a legal gray zone. They possess significant federal power inside an operational zone, and almost none outside of it.Because the government denies the existence of magic/monsters, Hunters cannot use "fighting monsters" as a legal defense in public court. Federal Concealed Carry exemption: Valid in all 50 states and Cook County. Hunters may carry restricted firearms concealed. Asset Seizure: Authority to confiscate "anomalous materials" (Cores, Artifacts) from civilians. Emergency Access: Right to bypass local police lines at confirmed Gate sites. Immunity (Conditional): Actions taken inside a sealed containment zone are classified and immune from local prosecution. The "7-11 Rule" (No Open Carry): Hunters may not open carry weapons in civilian areas. Walking into a convenience store in tactical gear with a sidearm visible is Disorderly Conduct. Local police will arrest you. The ARD will eventually release you, but you will face severe disciplinary action or license revocation. No Public Magic: Use of supernatural abilities in view of civilians or media is a Tier 1 Violation. Silence: Discussing Gate specifics with uncleared individuals triggers immediate contract termination and potential "indefinite detention." Civilian Safety: Collateral damage to civilians is not tolerated. Chicago PD: Aware of "Special Contractors" but generally resentful. They will arrest Hunters for public disturbances unless a Federal Liaison intervenes.

item.title: Overview
item.description: Aliases: The Guild (legacy slang), The Division, Hunters, Containment Parent Agency: Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Headquarters: Washington D.C. Chicago Regional HQ: O'Hare_MALC_Annex Legal Status: Classified Federal Law Enforcement / Contractor HybridTo detect, contain, and neutralize anomalous dimensional threats within the continental United States while maintaining public order and information security.The ARD does not exist on public organizational charts. "Hunters" are officially contractors for various shell agencies handling: Infrastructure stabilization (Gas leaks, sinkholes) Bio-hazard containment Counter-terrorism special weapons tactics Disaster relief The ARD is the thin line between the civilian population and the Gates. They operate under a doctrine of Denial and Containment. They are not superheroes; they are a paramilitary force managing a dimensional crisis that the public cannot know about.Most "Hunters" are Federal Contractors, not direct employees. This provides the government with plausible deniability. Contractors (PCs): Paid per mission/bounty, carry liability insurance, signed NDAs. Officers (NPCs): Direct federal agents, handle logistics, clean-up, and command.

item.title: Magic Rituals
item.description: To cast a spell, you must usually perform a ritual that involves gestures and speech. If you can’t perform the ritual, you can’t cast the spell! For instance, if the ritual for a spell requires you to speak, you cannot cast the spell if you are gagged or under a spell of silence.      The higher your skill with a spell, the easier it is to cast: it takes less time, requires less energy, and has less stringent ritual requirements. See the list below for details. In all cases, “skill” refers to base skill, not effective skill. The only modifier that matters here is the -5 for low mana, if applicable.Skill 9 or less – Ritual: You must have both hands and both feet free for elaborate ritual movements,and you must speak certain words of power in a firm voice. Time: Doubled. Cost: As listed. Skill 10-14 – Ritual: You must speak a few quiet words and make a gesture. Time: As listed. Cost: As listed. Skill 15-19 – Ritual: You must speak a word or two or make a small gesture (a couple of fingers are enough), but not necessarily both. You are allowed to move one yard per second while taking the Concentrate maneuver. Time: As listed. Cost: Reduced by 1. Skill 20-24 – Ritual: None! You simply stare into space as you concentrate. Time: Halved (round fractions up to the next second). Minimum casting time is still one second. Cost: Reduced by 2. Skill 25-29 – Ritual: None. Time: Divided by 4 (round up). Cost: Reduced by 3. Skill 30 or more – As above, but for every five levels of skill beyond skill 25 (that is, at levels 30, 35, 40, etc.), halve casting time again and reduce energy cost by one more point.  Certain spells always require a specific ritual. Such requirements override the rules above. For instance, high skill has no effect on the cost to cast Blocking spells (p. 241) or the time to cast Missile spells (p. 240).

item.title: Magery and Effect
item.description:
Talented mages may exceed the usual limits for spells that allow a finite number of “levels of effect” (dice of damage, bonuses to skill, etc.). The upper limit is the higher of the standard number of levels or the caster’s Magery level.
Example: Major Healing allows you to spend 1, 2, 3, or 4 energy points to heal 2, 4, 6, or 8 HP. It has four levels of effect. Magery 10 would let you revise this limit to 10 levels of effect – you could spend 1-10 energy points to heal 2-20 HP!
The GM is free not to use this rule if he thinks it would be unbalanced. Of course, if he puts a limit on the highest level of Magery available, this is not a problem!
item.guid: 10_System_Rules/11_Core_Gurps/General Abilities Article/Basic Set - Characters/Magic (Chapter 5)/Magery and Effect.md

item.title: Types of Disadvantages
item.description: Mental disadvantages originate from your mind or soul. They stay with you if your mind ends up in a new body. This category includes the vast majority of "magical," "psionic," and "spiritual" traits.Mental disadvantages are marked 3.Physical disadvantages are associated with your body. You can escape them by moving to a new body! If another mind occupies your body, the new owner gains your physical disadvantages.You can acquire a physical disadvantage during play, most likely due to accident or combat. In this case, you immediately suffer the bad effects of the disadvantage. Unlike starting disadvantages, however, physical handicaps acquired in play do not "give back" points with which to buy abilities - they just lower your point value!Example: If you start out blind, you start with an extra 50 points . . . but if an explosion blinds you during the game, you're just blind and that's that. Reduce your point total by 50 points to reflect your new disadvantage. You should not keep the same point total and take 50 points of compensating advantages!Physical disadvantages are marked 1.Social disadvantages are associated with your identity. Should it become important to know whether they go with mind or body, the GM's word is I final. Note that this category includes below-average Status, Wealth, and so I forth from Chapter 1.Social disadvantages are marked 2.The GM is the final judge of which category a disadvantage belongs in. It is possible to interpret certain disadvantages in more than one way!Exotic disadvantages are forbidden to normal humans. Nonhumans may acquire such traits from their racial template (see Chapter 7), but they still need the GM's permission to take additional exotic disadvantages.Exotic disadvantages are marked 4.Supernatural disadvantages are the result of divine intervention, magic, psionics, etc. With the GM's permission, anyone might be cursed in this way - but only if supernatural powers exist in the game world.Supernatural disadvantages are marked 5.Mundane disadvantages are everything else. They are inborn, acquired, or self-imposed handicaps that anyone might have. Mundane disadvantages are not marked in any special way. Assume that a disadvantage with neither 9 nor / is available to anyone.1234567890
item.guid: 10_System_Rules/11_Core_Gurps/General Abilities Article/Basic Set - Characters/Disadvantages/Types of Disadvantages.md

item.title: Self-Control for Mental Disadvantages
item.description: Many mental disadvantages do not affect you constantly - you may attempt to control your urges. An asterisk (*) appears next to the point cost of any disadvantage that offers a chance to resist. For each disadvantage like this, you must choose a selfcontrol number: the number you must roll on 3d to avoid giving in. This modifies point value as follows:You resist quite rarely (roll of 6 or less): 2 x listed cost.You resist fairly often (roll of 9 or less): 1.5 x listed cost.You resist quite often (roll of 12 or less): listed cost.You resist almost all the time (roll of 15 or less): 0.5 x listed cost.Drop all fractions (e.g., -22.5 points becomes -22 points).The "default" self-control number is 12: you must roll 12 or less on 3d to avoid giving in to your problem. This lets you use disadvantage costs as written. Choose a self-control number of 15 if you wish to have a tendency toward a disadvantage instead of a full-blown case. A self-control number of 9 will regularly limit your options. A self-control number of 6 can be crippling (especially with genuine psychiatric problems).Note your self-control number in parentheses after the name of the disadvantage on your character sheet. For instance, if you can resist Berserk on a roll of 9 or less, write this as "Berserk (9)."In circumstances that are likely to trigger your problem, you may opt to roll 3d against your self-control number to see whether your disadvantage actually affects you. If you roll less than or equal to this number, you resist your disadvantage - this time. Otherwise, you suffer the listed effects. This is called a self-control roll.Like all success rolls, self-control rolls arc subject to modifiers. Exceptionally mild or severe stimuli can give bonuses or penalties. Drugs and afflictions can make you more or less likely to give in. Other disadvantages can make you irritable, reducing your odds of resisting. See the disadvantage descriptions for details.Example: Your self-control number is 15, but you are in a highly stressful situation that gives -5 to your self-control roll. You must roll 10 or less to resist your disadvantage. You never have to try a self-control roll - you can always give in willingly, and it is good roleplaying to do so. However, there will be times when you really need to resist your urges, and that is what the roll is for. Be aware that if you attempt self-control rolls too often, the GM may penalize you for bad roleplaying by awarding you fewer earned points.Optionally, the GM may permit you to use one unspent character point to "buy" an automatic success on a selfcontrol roll. Points spent this way are gone for good, but there will be times when staying on the straight and narrow is worth the sacrifice. In this case, the GM should not penalize you for bad roleplaying, because you are penalizing yourself!Note that high Will helps you make Fright Checks and resist supernatural emotion control, but it does not improve self-control rolls - not even for disadvantages with effects identical to these things. Mental disadvantages represent an aspect of your personality that you cannot simply will (or reason) away. This is part of what makes them disadvantages!
item.guid: 10_System_Rules/11_Core_Gurps/General Abilities Article/Basic Set - Characters/Disadvantages/Self-Control for Mental Disadvantages.md

item.description: If a single rapid-fire attack scores multiple hits, a successful Dodge roll lets you avoid one hit, plus additional hits equal to your margin of success. item.title: Gurps Creature
item.description: Creating MonstersJust about any creature from any GURPS supplement can work as a dungeon denizen. If it wasn’t designed for fantasy, simply change the special effects. For instance, an alien that zips through space, blasting people with psionic pyrokinesis, becomes a demon that flies through the air, blasting people with magic fireballs. Simple!Like traps, monsters are fun to design. For each homemade monster, the GM should have enough information to resolve not just combat, but all of the situations discussed under Monsters (p. 9). Don’t bother building monsters with character points! The following details will more than suffice:Attack (Skill or Resistance): For instance, “Bite (14): 1d+2 cutting” or “Death Gaze (15 vs. HT): Heart Attack (p. B429).” Bites inflict thrust-1, while strikers (horns, scorpion tails, etc.) deliver thrust at +1/die; either may be cutting, crushing, or impaling. Limbs do thrust-1 (thrust for a hind limb); they may be crushing (+1/die with Blunt Claws), or cutting or impaling (+1/die with Long Talons). Natural attacks often benefit from Striking ST that raises damage; cutting and impaling ones can carry follow-up venom (note resistance roll and damage). Resistance and effects for supernatural attacks are arbitrary. Give each attack its own line.Traits: Advantages or disadvantages important in dungeon fantasy, such as Acute Senses (for noticing sneaky delvers), Constriction Attack, Indomitable (for a monster that can’t be influenced), Magic Resistance, Regeneration, and Unfazeable (for a fearless creature). Don’t bother repeating DR, Innate Attacks, etc., already noted above.Skills: Relevant skills, especially Brawling (at DX+2 or above, this gives +1 damage per die with natural attacks) and Stealth.Class: Animal (Giant if huge or Dire if mutant; affected by Animal Handling and Animal spells), Construct (incorruptible magical servant), Demon (hostile extradimensional creature subject to the Banish spell), Elder Thing (hostile extradimensional creature not subject to Banish), Elemental (subject to Banish and Control Elemental), Faerie (freewilled creature of magic), Hybrid (as Animal, but shares traits of two or more beasts and requires a special subset of Animal spells), Mundane (any living thing that isn’t Animal, Plant, or Slime and that has vital areas, like goblins and generic mouth-and-tentacles creatures), Plant (affected by Plant spells), Slime (diffuse, IQ 0 ooze that’s immune to most Animal and Plant spells), or Undead (can be turned with True Faith). This is important for Higher Purpose advantages and when choosing the skill used to recognize the thing (see Recognition, p. 9).
